imageInfo.note: Detail of the dedication page of the Bible moralisée of Toledo, the "Bible of Saint Louis": this leaf is in the Morgan Library & Museum, New York (MS M.240, fol. 8r), and the rest of the Bible is in Toledo Cathedral. The full page shows Blanche of Castile enthroned opposite the young king, with a cleric and a scribe below. It was painted in Louis's lifetime, while he was in his teens, but it is a conventional royal image, not a likeness. The Morgan dates the manuscript about 1227–1234; some scholars allow about 1225–1245.

overview: Louis IX was king of France, leader of the Seventh and Eighth Crusades, and later a canonized royal saint. His crusading campaigns in Egypt and Tunis both ended in failure or death, yet shaped Capetian sanctity and monarchy.
Louis is remembered as a saintly king, but his crusading record also shows the limits of piety, logistics, and royal resources in thirteenth-century warfare.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Louis IX was king of France, leader of the Seventh and Eighth Crusades, and later a canonized royal saint. His crusading campaigns in Egypt and Tunis both ended in failure or death, yet shaped Capetian sanctity and monarchy.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Louis was born into the Capetian dynasty and ruled first under the regency of his mother Blanche of Castile, whose government protected royal authority during his minority.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Louis IX of France became Saint Louis, and his remembered character is shaped by a sanctity that was, unusually, well attested in his own lifetime by those who knew him. The intimate memoir of his friend Jean de Joinville presents a king of genuine and rigorous piety — given to prayer, fasting, and charity, washing the feet of the poor, and dispensing justice in person beneath an oak at Vincennes — combined with personal warmth, humour, and an unbending sense of moral duty.

His devotion was real and severe, expressed in two crusades that both ended in failure and, on the first, in his own capture and ransom in Egypt; he died on the second, at Tunis. Joinville's affectionate portrait also records a king of conscience who could be harsh in matters of faith — stern toward blasphemy and hostile to the Jews of his realm — so the sanctity carried a hard edge that an honest account must include.

Because the fullest portrait comes from a devoted friend and from the process that canonised him, the holiness is emphasised, yet Joinville's candour about the king's human qualities gives it unusual credibility. He is remembered as the model Christian king — just, devout, and personally humble, but also rigid and uncompromising in his faith — one of the few medieval rulers whose saintly reputation rests on the testimony of those who lived beside him.

contentSections.title: As crusader king of France
paragraphs: Louis led the Seventh Crusade to Egypt, captured Damietta, and was defeated and captured after Mansurah. He later spent years in the eastern Mediterranean strengthening crusader defenses before launching the Tunis crusade in 1270.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Louis died of disease near Tunis in 1270 during the Eighth Crusade. His body and relics became central to Capetian sacred kingship.

contentSections.title: Legacy
